description: Companion to trials.json: notable ME/CFS research papers (pathomechanism, biomarkers, drug targets, treatment/trial results, genetics), prioritising Wirth/Scheibenbogen but NOT Germany-restricted. Seeded 2026-06-26 with a one-time comprehensive backfill of landmark + recent work (each verified via DOI/PubMed); routine runs add newer papers going forward. Shown on the dashboard's Papers tab. STYLE: write 'summary' and 'why' for a layperson — plain language, short sentences, jargon only where unavoidable and explained in a few words. Confirm each via DOI/journal/preprint before recording; never fabricate.

papers.title: Involvement of autoantibodies against G protein-coupled receptors in post-COVID condition and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Azcue N, Prada A, Del Pino R, Acera M, Fernández-Valle T, Ayo-Mentxakatorre N, Pérez-Concha T, Murueta-Goyena A, Lafuente JV, López de Munain A, Ruiz Irastorza G, Ribacoba L, Gabilondo I, Tijero-Merino B, Gómez-Esteban JC
papers.summary: Researchers measured autoantibodies — antibodies that mistakenly attack the body's own receptors for stress hormones and nerve signals — in the blood of 96 people with post-COVID condition, 59 with ME/CFS, and 36 healthy people. People with ME/CFS had higher levels of one such antibody (targeting a stress-hormone receptor called beta-2-adrenergic), and higher antibody levels went along with worse autonomic-nervous-system problems (like poor control of blood pressure and heart rate) and slower thinking speed.
papers.why: Adds another data point to the idea that misdirected antibodies attacking the body's own receptors help drive ME/CFS symptoms — the same idea behind Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption trials (IMPACT, IA-Surv) that filter these antibodies out of the blood, though this is a different, Spanish (Basque Country) research group, not Wirth or Scheibenbogen themselves.
papers.notes: Sci Rep, published online May 5, 2026. PMID 42082542. Basque Country/Spain group (Biocruces Bizkaia / UPV-EHU, incl. López de Munain, Gabilondo). n=96 post-COVID, 59 ME/CFS, 36 healthy controls; anti-beta2-adrenergic-receptor autoantibody levels elevated in ME/CFS vs healthy, correlated with autonomic dysfunction and processing-speed measures. Distinct from the already-tracked azcue-2026-postcovid-mecfs-convergence entry (different journal/DOI/focus, overlapping but not identical author list). Backfilled this run — publication date (May 5) is close to the edge of the ~3-month recency window and was missed by prior daily sweeps; confirmed independently via Europe PMC REST API (title/authorString/journalTitle/pubYear/firstPublicationDate/PMID/DOI all match). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Also screened and excluded this run: Abanades et al. 'Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy to Restore Mitochondrial Function in ME/CFS and Fibromyalgia' (Preprints.org, posted Jul 20, 2026, doi 10.20944/preprints202607.1446.v1) — a narrative review/future-trial-proposal with no new patient data, posted to Preprints.org, a lower-tier preprint venue only accepted in this database as an exception for Wirth-authored papers per ROUTINE.md; not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored, so held to the standard medRxiv/bioRxiv/peer-reviewed bar and not added.

papers.title: Circulating extracellular vesicles-microRNAs as potential biomarkers for the identification of ME/CFS: differentiating fatigue-related conditions
papers.authors: Eguchi A, Kuratsune H, Nakatomi Y, Yasui T, Nakagawa R, Watanabe Y, Fukuda S
papers.summary: Researchers compared tiny particles that cells release into the blood (extracellular vesicles) and the small RNA snippets they carry (microRNAs) in people with ME/CFS, people with ordinary chronic fatigue, and people with depression. ME/CFS patients had a distinct pattern of these particles and about 62 microRNAs that stood out compared to the other groups, pointing to disrupted nerve-cell and cell-structure pathways.
papers.why: Adds to a growing set of blood-based candidate markers that could eventually help doctors tell ME/CFS apart from look-alike conditions like depression or general tiredness, something there is currently no reliable test for — though this is a small, early exploratory study that needs replication in larger groups.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 24(1):979, published Jul 27, 2026. PMID 42533331. Osaka group (Eguchi/Kuratsune/Nakatomi/Watanabe/Fukuda), small exploratory cohort comparing ME/CFS vs. idiopathic chronic fatigue vs. depression by EV-microRNA profiling; ~62 differentially expressed microRNAs (incl. miR-21-5p, let-7f-5p, miR-26b-5p, miR-20a-5p) implicated in neuronal/cytoskeletal pathways. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed independently via PubMed record (PMID 42533331) and Springer/J Transl Med publisher page redirect from the DOI.

papers.title: Molecular hydrogen as a treatment for ME/CFS: a mini-review of clinical evidence and mechanistic rationale
papers.authors: Friedberg F, LeBaron TW
papers.summary: This mini-review looks at hydrogen-rich water — ordinary water with extra dissolved hydrogen gas — as a possible ME/CFS treatment. It calms harmful cell damage (antioxidant effect), reduces inflammation, and may help the cell's energy factories (mitochondria) work better. Three small early studies found it feasible and modestly helpful for fatigue, with mild side effects.
papers.why: A low-cost, low-risk supplement with early but weak evidence for reducing fatigue — worth watching, though the studies so far are small, not blinded, and rely on patients' own symptom reports rather than objective measurements.
papers.notes: Published Mar 18, 2026 (Frontiers in Medicine, vol. 13, Translational Medicine section) — newly found this run (missed by prior searches, similar to the earlier-missed wirth-2026-hypovolemia-review). Narrative mini-review of 3 small pilot studies (same research team) of hydrogen-rich water in ME/CFS; authors call for larger, blinded trials with objective biomarkers. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page. Also screened and excluded this run (fails papers scope — healthcare-delivery/care-pathway studies, not pathomechanism/biomarker/drug-target/treatment-trial/genetics): Aung/Scuffell et al., 'General Practice Perspectives on Post-Infection Conditions' (medRxiv, Jul 17 2026, UK GP scoping review + survey) and Burchardi/Scheibenbogen et al., 'LCovB' study protocol (PLoS One, Jul 9 2026, Charité post-COVID care-pathway mixed-methods study) — both are care-delivery protocols/surveys, not biomedical mechanism or treatment-trial-results papers. Also excluded: Ben Amar et al. 'epigenetic signatures in chronic pain' (Epigenomics, Jul 22 2026) — general chronic-pain topic, not ME/CFS-specific. Also excluded: Kuns et al. 'The State of Chronic Fatigue' PEM systematic review (Arch Phys Med Rehabil 107(5):e191, doi 10.1016/j.apmr.2026.02.468) — appears to be a conference-abstract-supplement entry (page 'e191'), not a full peer-reviewed article, so held to a lower-confidence bar than the mini-review above; not entered pending the full paper.

papers.title: Multimodal approach to identify neuropsychophysiological subgroups in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and their relevance for rehabilitation
papers.authors: Dooms Y, Qiu L, Coppieters I, Vergaelen E, Claes S, Dupont P, Hehl M, Cuypers K, Engler H, Dombrowski K, Verbeke K, Van den Bergh O, Raes J, Van Oudenhove L, Van Den Houte M, Bogaerts K
papers.summary: This is a study protocol (a research plan, not results yet) describing a planned Belgian study that will test 115 ME/CFS patients and 55 healthy people with a wide mix of measurements — inflammation markers, brain scans for inflammation, nervous-system function, gut bacteria, and stress-hormone responses — then follow patients through a rehabilitation programme to see which measurements predict who improves.
papers.why: Aims to sort ME/CFS patients into biological subgroups so future treatment (including rehabilitation) can be matched to what's actually driving each patient's illness, rather than one-size-fits-all — worth watching for when results are published.
papers.notes: Published online Jul 6, 2026 (eCollection Oct 2026). Study protocol only (n=115 ME/CFS, 55 controls planned), KU Leuven/Belgian group. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Elsevier/ScienceDirect publisher page.

papers.title: Agreement and reliability between the two-day 6-minute incremental step test and two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test in post COVID-19 condition for assessing post-exertional malaise: The REVEAL-study
papers.authors: Bomans S, Michotte N, El M'Rabet I, Jimenez Garcia B, Leemans L, Janssens P, Hanon S, De Waele E, Beckwée D
papers.summary: Researchers tested whether a simpler, cheaper 6-minute stepping test, done on two separate days, could replace the demanding two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET — a treadmill/bike test measuring oxygen use) for detecting post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity) in 25 people with post-COVID condition. The simpler step test only partly agreed with the CPET results, especially for oxygen-use and muscle-symptom measures, so it isn't yet reliable enough to fully substitute for the more demanding test.
papers.why: Finding an easier, less exhausting way to objectively measure PEM would make it much simpler to run future ME/CFS and post-COVID drug trials — this study is a needed reality-check showing the simpler option still needs refinement before it can be trusted.
papers.notes: Published Jul 14, 2026. Crossover design, n=25, one-month washout, Belgian group (UZ Brussel). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via PLOS ONE publisher page.

papers.title: Microstructural alterations in brain tissue of ME/CFS and long COVID using diffusion tensor imaging and diffusion kurtosis imaging
papers.authors: Singh TB, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Barnden L, Eaton-Fitch N, Huynh TH, Inderyas M, Thapaliya K
papers.summary: Using two advanced brain-scan techniques that map the tiny fibres connecting brain regions (diffusion tensor and diffusion kurtosis imaging), researchers compared brain structure in 37 people with ME/CFS, 19 with long COVID, and 27 healthy people. Both illnesses showed subtle differences from healthy brains, but in different areas and patterns — including changes in a motor-planning region and in the bundle of fibres linking the brain's two hemispheres — suggesting ME/CFS and long COVID are not simply the same condition at the brain-structure level.
papers.why: One of the first studies to directly compare brain wiring in ME/CFS versus long COVID rather than each against healthy people alone, adding evidence the two conditions may need to be studied and treated as biologically distinct rather than interchangeable.
papers.notes: Published Jul 17, 2026. Griffith University (Australia) neuroimaging group (Marshall-Gradisnik/Barnden/Thapaliya) — a recurring credible ME/CFS research team already in this database (thapaliya-2026-glymphatic-dti-alps, sasso-2026-trpm3-nkcell). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page.

papers.title: Handgrip strength in children, adolescents, and young adults with suspected myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Mihatsch L, Schartner L, de Luna JL, Höhler C, Bucka L, Lovrenovic L, Eidenschink S, Schmuck B, Bienemann V, Christa C, Mittelstraß K, Hausruckinger A, Warlitz C, Michel K, Gerrer K, Freitag H, Scheibenbogen C, Pricoco R, Behrends U
papers.summary: Researchers measured hand-grip strength twice, an hour apart, in 147 young people (aged 10-25) being evaluated for ME/CFS and compared them with 83 healthy peers. The patients' grip strength and how it changed between the two tests differed from the healthy group, showing a real, measurable drop in muscle function — but the test alone could not reliably tell ME/CFS apart from other conditions that also cause tiredness.
papers.why: From Carmen Scheibenbogen's group: offers a simple, cheap, repeatable physical test that could serve as an objective way to track post-exertional muscle decline in children and teenagers for future drug trials, even though it can't yet stand alone as a diagnostic test.
papers.notes: Published online Jul 15, 2026. Pediatric/young-adult ME/CFS evaluation cohort (Charité/TU München group, incl. Behrends and Pricoco), 147 patients aged 10-25 vs 83 controls; two grip-strength sessions 60 minutes apart. Scheibenbogen is a co-author — HIGH PRIORITY. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/journal/date match).

papers.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
papers.authors: Gile B, Bulbule S, Toriola MA, Ruan BT, Marium S, Benko A, Grach S, Mueller M, Bateman L, Bell J, Yellman B, Berner J, Chheda B, Kaufman D, Gottschalk G, Roy A
papers.summary: In a small ongoing trial without a placebo group, ME/CFS patients took low-dose rapamycin (a drug that calms an overactive cell-growth signal) for three months. Blood and immune tests showed shifts in energy-related chemicals, calmer brain immune cells, better-working cellular batteries (mitochondria), and patients reported less fatigue.
papers.why: One of the few ME/CFS drug studies to show a treatment changing measurable body chemistry alongside symptom improvement, giving a testable biological reason — not just patient reports — to pursue rapamycin as a treatment lead.
papers.notes: PMID 42432754; registered as NCT06257420 (phase II observational pilot, Bateman Horne Center / Simmaron Research, USA). Published online Jul 10, 2026. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via journal DOI record.

papers.title: In Search of Lost Volume: The Potential Causes of Hypovolemia in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth argues that people with ME/CFS often have too little fluid in their blood vessels (hypovolemia), caused by broken salt-and-water retention signals in the body, leaky small blood vessels, and starved muscle cells pulling fluid out of the blood during activity.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure): ties together low blood volume, dizziness on standing, and the post-exertional crash (a crash after activity) into one physical explanation, reinforcing the case for his group's muscle/circulation-focused treatment approach — but it's an early, not-yet-peer-reviewed hypothesis paper, so treat it as a working idea pending review.
papers.notes: Solo-author hypothesis/review paper posted Feb 2026 (v1) on Preprints.org — newly found this run (missed by prior searches). Included as an exception per ROUTINE.md's Wirth HIGH-priority provision, same lower-tier preprint-venue caveat as the already-tracked wirth-2026-connective-tissue-laxity. Not yet peer-reviewed.

papers.title: The efficacy of exercise in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Zhao L, Gou B, Zhang M
papers.summary: Combining results from 17 controlled trials with almost 2,000 ME/CFS patients, exercise programmes improved fatigue, sleep, and quality of life, but did not meaningfully improve heart/lung fitness or physical capacity.
papers.why: Exercise therapy is a historically controversial topic in ME/CFS because overexertion can trigger post-exertional malaise (a crash after activity). This large pooled analysis suggests exercise may ease some symptoms but is not a fix for the underlying physical limitation, supporting a cautious, symptom-management role rather than a cure.
papers.notes: Online Apr 15, 2026; print Aug 2026 (Vol 207). Meta-analysis of 17 RCTs, n=1,944. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Wang S, Ren J, Fang S, Hao Q, Zhang YQ, Kong L, Fang M
papers.summary: Analysing 16 trials of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT, a talk therapy) for ME/CFS, guided self-help and one-on-one CBT reduced fatigue right after treatment. The specific ingredients that helped were goal-setting and acceptance-based techniques, while just teaching patients facts about the illness (psychoeducation) alone was possibly unhelpful.
papers.why: CBT is another historically contentious ME/CFS treatment. Rather than a blanket 'CBT works' or 'CBT doesn't work' claim, this pinpoints which specific ingredients may help versus backfire — useful for designing better-targeted psychological support alongside biomedical treatment.
papers.notes: Brain Behav 16(6), Jun 2026 (online May 31, 2026). Component network meta-analysis of 16 trials. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Efficacy of acupuncture-based traditional Chinese medicine therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Li Y, Liang G, Xiao T, Xu L
papers.summary: Combining 8 trials with 715 patients, acupuncture reduced overall, physical, and mental fatigue more than control treatments, with no difference in side effects — though the authors themselves caution the trials were small and of uneven quality.
papers.why: Adds acupuncture to the list of non-drug approaches with some trial evidence for ME/CFS fatigue, though the low-confidence evidence base (small, uneven-quality trials, flagged by the authors themselves) means it should not be over-weighted against biomedical treatment approaches.
papers.notes: Front Neurol 17, Jun 24, 2026. Meta-analysis of 8 trials, n=715. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) gene expression signatures for the identification of compounds targeting metabolism
papers.authors: Dehlia A, Alizada Z, Guthridge MA
papers.summary: Researchers combined two separate sets of ME/CFS patients' gene-activity data to find a shared pattern of 46 genes that behave differently in ME/CFS, then used a computer search to find existing drugs that might reverse that pattern. Three of the four candidate drugs — including pioglitazone, an already-approved diabetes medicine — gave a modest boost to energy production when tested on muscle cells grown in the lab.
papers.why: Flags specific already-approved drugs that target how cells produce energy, which could be tested in ME/CFS patients faster than developing a brand-new drug, and adds independent computational support to the energy-production theory of ME/CFS.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted Research Square Jul 5, 2026. Datasets GSE14577 and GSE227375; CMap L1000 drug-repurposing analysis; candidate compounds pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, tideglusib, MHY1485 tested on mouse myoblasts for mitochondrial membrane potential — all but rosiglitazone showed a modest significant increase. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC record.

papers.title: The physio-affective symptoms of Long COVID are strongly predicted by the severity of the acute infectious phase, and lowered antioxidants, nitric oxide, and alanine transaminase levels
papers.authors: Maes M, Tunvirachaisakul C, Semeão LdO, Michelin AP, Matsumoto AK, Brinholi FF, Barbosa DS, Zhang Y, Sodsai P, Hirankarn N, Almulla AF
papers.summary: Followed 71 long-COVID patients for six months and found that mood symptoms, CFS/ME-type fatigue symptoms, breathing problems, and nervous-system symptoms all rise and fall together as one combined package rather than being separate problems. How severe a person's original COVID infection was — including low levels of antioxidants and nitric oxide, molecules that help protect cells and blood vessels — strongly predicted how bad this combined symptom package became.
papers.why: Suggests it may be possible to predict, from measurements taken during the original COVID infection, which patients are heading toward the more severe, ME/CFS-like form of long COVID — useful for identifying who to watch closely or treat early.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted Research Square Jun 28, 2026 (indexed Jul 2). Same Maes-led international group as donchev-2026-gut-microbiome-mecfs-longcovid and petrov-2026-monocyte-dc-immunophenotyping already in this database. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC record.

papers.title: Risk factors for severe post-COVID condition in children, adolescents, and young adults
papers.authors: Donath Q, Haegele M, Schindler D, Welzhofer T, Christa C, Grabbe A, Leone A, Ilhan C, Weidmann C, Eberhartinger M, Bechtold S, Bursch N, Wolf H, Hieber H, Peo LC, Bucka LA, Stojanov S, Warlitz C, Alberer M, Gerrer K, Hausruckinger A, Mittelstrass K, Wendtner CM, Hoechstetter MA, Grübl A, Toepfner N, Pricoco R, Scheibenbogen C, Mihatsch LL, Behrends U
papers.summary: In a German study of 120 young people (7–25 years old) with long-lasting COVID symptoms, having 12 or more symptoms during the original infection, plus dizziness or fainting-type symptoms (a sign of the body struggling to regulate blood flow when standing up), strongly predicted who would go on to develop the most severe, disabling form of the illness — 24% of whom were ultimately diagnosed with ME/CFS.
papers.why: Gives doctors an early-warning checklist for spotting which children are at risk of the most severe, ME/CFS-associated outcome after COVID, potentially enabling earlier intervention. Scheibenbogen is a co-author — HIGH PRIORITY.
papers.notes: PMID 42082813. Eur J Pediatr 185(5):344. Published May 4, 2026. German multi-centre paediatric long-COVID cohort (n=120, ages 7-25). Scheibenbogen (Charité) co-author — HIGH PRIORITY. Confirmed via PubMed record (full author list, abstract, DOI).

papers.title: Disrupted glymphatic function and its relationship with sleep and cognitive impairment in ME/CFS assessed via DTI-ALPS
papers.authors: Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Inderyas M, Barnden L
papers.summary: Using a brain-scan technique that measures how well the brain clears waste while a person sleeps, researchers found that people with ME/CFS (31 patients vs 27 healthy people) have a noticeably weaker brain 'cleaning' system than healthy people, especially on the right side of the brain — and those with worse sleep and worse concentration/memory problems had the weakest waste-clearance.
papers.why: Points to a concrete physical mechanism — sluggish brain waste removal during sleep — that could help explain the brain fog and sleep disruption common in ME/CFS, and gives researchers a new measurable target for future biomarker or treatment studies.
papers.notes: Frontiers in Neuroscience, published Jun 19, 2026. Griffith University (Australia) neuroimaging group (Marshall-Gradisnik/Barnden), a recurring credible ME/CFS research team. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page (title/authors/date/DOI/abstract).

papers.title: Immunoadsorption Versus Sham Treatment for Post-COVID Syndrome: A Randomised Sham-Controlled Crossover Trial
papers.authors: Stortz M, Kommer A, Meineck M, Boedecker-Lips SC, Claßen P, Tomalla V, Rausch F, Lang LS, Wild PS, Schmidtmann I, Weinmann A, Kraus D, Weinmann-Menke J
papers.summary: In this German trial (Mainz), 40 people with long-term post-COVID symptoms and high levels of self-attacking antibodies had those antibodies filtered out of their blood (immunoadsorption), compared with a fake (sham) version of the same procedure. The real treatment did remove the antibodies as intended, but patients did not feel any better than those who got the sham treatment, and side effects were more common with the real treatment.
papers.why: This is a rigorous, placebo-controlled negative result for a treatment approach (removing 'self-attacking' antibodies) that other German trials — including Scheibenbogen's — are also testing in post-COVID/ME-CFS, so it's an important caution: filtering out these antibodies doesn't automatically translate into symptom relief, at least in this dosing/design.
papers.notes: Lancet Reg Health Eur, Vol 67 (Aug 2026 print; e-pub Jun 11, 2026). University Medical Center Mainz (IAMPOCO trial). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Elsevier publisher page and Europe PMC record.

papers.title: Insights into Pathophysiological Pathways in ME/CFS Through Genetic Correlation and Mendelian Randomization
papers.authors: Wielscher M, Vincenzi L, Weninger WP, Schernhammer ES
papers.summary: Using genetic data from the large DecodeME study (over 15,000 people with ME/CFS), researchers looked for genes shared between ME/CFS and other conditions, and tested whether some blood markers might actually cause ME/CFS risk rather than just being correlated with it. They found that having naturally more mitochondrial DNA (the energy-factory part of cells) seemed protective, while two markers of inflammation and blood-clotting activity seemed to raise risk.
papers.why: This is genetic evidence — not just an association in sick patients — pointing to cellular energy production and low-grade inflammation/clotting as likely causes rather than side effects of ME/CFS, which supports the biological rationale behind drugs targeting mitochondria or clotting/inflammation.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. v1 posted Apr 10, 2026; v2 Apr 21, 2026. Medical University of Vienna group. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Direct Research Square fetch blocked (403); confirmed via Europe PMC record (title/authors/DOI/date/key finding) plus preprint-report secondary summary.

papers.title: Global and local genetic overlap among ME/CFS, irritable bowel syndrome and psychiatric traits: a hypothesis-generating analysis
papers.authors: Lee JH
papers.summary: This genetic study compared ME/CFS with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), depression, and loneliness using large genetic databases. Overall, ME/CFS shared a lot of genetic background with IBS and depression, but when the analysis zoomed in on specific spots in the genome, very little of that overlap held up — and the genes linked to ME/CFS risk were concentrated in nerve cells (including gut nerve cells), not in depression-related brain circuits.
papers.why: Even though ME/CFS, IBS and depression often occur together and can look similar, this suggests ME/CFS has its own distinct genetic roots in the nervous system rather than simply being a form of depression — relevant to arguments that ME/CFS deserves biomedical treatment research, not just psychiatric care.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted Jun 10, 2026. Single-author analysis built on DecodeME summary statistics. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC record.

papers.title: Perioperative outcomes in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome undergoing general anesthesia: a retrospective matched-pair study
papers.authors: Steinkirchner FM, Kaufmann CK, Kraus RF, Käss M, Schieffer E, Graf BM, Lassen C, Kimmerling V, Dejaco A
papers.summary: Looking back at hospital records for 15 people with ME/CFS who had surgery under general anaesthesia, matched against 15 similar patients without ME/CFS, the study found blood pressure and heart rate during surgery were similarly well controlled in both groups — but people with ME/CFS had noticeably more pain afterward and needed stronger pain medication more often.
papers.why: This is practical safety information for patients and doctors: general anaesthesia itself appears manageable in ME/CFS, but post-surgery pain management may need extra attention — useful for anyone with ME/CFS facing an operation, even though it doesn't point to a new drug or trial.
papers.notes: Originally a medRxiv preprint (posted Apr 7, 2026, doi 10.64898/2026.04.06.26348924), now formally published in peer-reviewed BMC Anesthesiology (Jul 16, 2026, PMID 42464211, doi 10.1186/s12871-026-04102-5) — journal/date/link updated 2026-07-19 to the peer-reviewed version. German group (University Hospital Regensburg). Small sample (n=15 pairs); post-exertional malaise not tracked, noted by the authors as a limitation. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via PubMed record.

papers.title: Association between light exposure patterns and multidimensional health outcomes in individuals with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Cambras T, Domingo JC, Sanmartín-Sentañes R, Alegre-Martín J, Castro-Marrero J
papers.summary: Using a week of wrist-worn light and activity sensors in 100 ME/CFS patients and 56 healthy people, researchers found four patterns of daily light exposure; patients with a 'healthy' pattern (stable light during the day) had less fatigue and better sleep than patients with poor daytime light exposure.
papers.why: Suggests that how much natural light a patient gets during the day is linked to how bad their symptoms are, pointing to light exposure as a simple, low-cost target that could be tested as part of future ME/CFS treatment plans.
papers.notes: PMID 42399727. Published Jul 3, 2026. Spanish group (Vall d'Hebron / Universitat de Barcelona). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via publisher page (Springer/J Transl Med).

papers.title: Human Endogenous Retroviruses in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Emerging Roles in Pathogenesis, Immunity, Biomarkers and Therapeutics
papers.authors: Perera KD, Oltra E, Carding SR
papers.summary: A review paper explains how ancient virus fragments built into our own DNA long ago (human endogenous retroviruses, or HERVs) normally stay silent, but common infections like Epstein-Barr virus, HHV-6 or COVID-19 may switch some of them back on, and this reactivation could help drive the immune problems and brain inflammation seen in ME/CFS.
papers.why: Proposes a concrete biological trigger — reactivated 'fossil viruses' inside our own genome — that could explain why an infection can lead to long-term illness, and suggests measuring which of these HERVs are switched on could become a diagnostic test or way to track treatment response.
papers.notes: Int J Mol Sci 27(10):4309. Published May 12, 2026. Review article; Oltra's group (CEU Cardenal Herrera Univ., Spain) and Carding (Quadram Institute, UK). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via MDPI publisher page.

papers.title: Comprehensive Immunophenotyping of Monocytes and Dendritic Cells Suggests Distinct Pathophysiology in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Long COVID
papers.authors: Petrov S, Bozhkova M, Ivanovska M, Kalfova T, Dudova D, Todorova Y, Dimitrova R, Murdjeva M, Taskov H, Nikolova M, Maes M
papers.summary: Detailed immune-cell testing on blood from 103 ME/CFS patients, 63 long COVID patients and 41 healthy people found the two illnesses look different at the immune-cell level: long COVID showed signs of an immune system still fighting but wearing out, while ME/CFS showed a more suppressed, poorly-coordinated immune response.
papers.why: Even though ME/CFS and long COVID often look similar to patients, this suggests their underlying immune problems differ — meaning treatments effective for one may not automatically work for the other, an important consideration when designing future drug trials.
papers.notes: Int J Mol Sci 27(10):4488. Published May 17, 2026. Bulgarian/international group (Plovdiv Medical University) incl. Michael Maes. Originally posted as medRxiv preprint 2026.04.10.26350613. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated.

papers.title: Higher-order brain processes, rather than early processing, underlie sensory problems in ME/CFS: evidence from ERPs
papers.authors: Kumar S, Veldhuis A, Yazdani F
papers.summary: Using brain-wave recordings (ERPs) during sound tests in 31 people with ME/CFS and 30 healthy people, basic sound processing in the brain was normal, but a later brain signal linked to attention and mental effort was weaker in the ME/CFS patients.
papers.why: Suggests sensory overload in ME/CFS comes from how the brain manages attention and higher-level processing rather than from broken basic senses — pointing future treatments toward this higher-level brain function rather than the sense organs themselves.
papers.notes: PMID 42396162. Published June 18, 2026. Confirmed via the Frontiers in Media article page. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated.

papers.title: iPSC-Derived Myogenic Progenitor Cells from People with ME/CFS Reveal Altered Genes and Pathways with Drug Repurposing Potential
papers.authors: Nguyen D, Truong TTT, Panizzutti B, Ellis M, Spolding B, Swinton C, Bortolasci CC, Bryce J, Smith J, Field C, Liu ZS, Kim JH, Berk M, Walder K
papers.summary: Muscle precursor cells grown in the lab from stem cells taken from ME/CFS patients showed altered activity in genes involved in cell division, DNA repair, immune response and muscle structure, and used certain nutrients for energy differently than cells from healthy people.
papers.why: Lab evidence that ME/CFS muscle cells are genuinely different at a molecular level, not just 'deconditioned' — and the authors computationally flag 22 existing drugs (including leflunomide, melatonin and midodrine) as candidates that could be tested faster than developing a new drug, though this is an early, not-yet-peer-reviewed preprint using a lab stem-cell model.
papers.notes: Posted Research Square Jun 16, 2026 (v1, single author Nguyen D); revised to v2 Jul 21, 2026 adding a full multi-author byline (Deakin University/Barwon Health, Australia group incl. senior authors Michael Berk and Ken Walder) — same study/DOI family, no material change to findings (still 22 drug-repurposing candidates incl. leflunomide, melatonin, midodrine). Authors/date/link updated 2026-07-22 to reflect v2. Still not yet peer-reviewed. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated.

papers.title: Development and initial content validation of the Vienna Post-Exertional Malaise Questionnaire: an iterative mixed-methods study
papers.authors: Pimminger T, Ahrens-Schwabe A, Fragner T, Brandl T, Kotzian S, Wüst RC, Waldhör T, Kapan A
papers.summary: An Austrian team worked with patients and experts through several rounds of feedback to build a new 13-question survey that specifically measures post-exertional malaise (PEM) — the 'crash' after activity that is the hallmark symptom of ME/CFS.
papers.why: A patient-informed, purpose-built way to measure PEM could improve diagnosis and become a standard outcome measure in future ME/CFS drug trials, though full scientific validation is still pending.
papers.notes: Posted Research Square Jun 16, 2026. Not yet peer-reviewed. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/author/date match). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated.

papers.title: Therapeutic plasma exchange and immunomodulatory strategies in post-infectious syndromes: A review of immune dysregulation in PTLDS, long COVID, ME/CFS, and PANS/PANDAS
papers.authors: Kaplan G
papers.summary: A review article argues that ME/CFS, long COVID, chronic Lyme disease, and certain childhood post-infectious conditions all involve the immune system misfiring in similar ways — including inflammation and self-attacking antibodies — and discusses whether blood-filtering treatments like plasma exchange could help.
papers.why: Argues that past large trials of these therapies underperformed because they enrolled patients without using biomarkers to pick who was likely to benefit — a lesson for how future ME/CFS drug trials should select patients.
papers.notes: PMID 42391726. Published online Jun 26, 2026 (print issue Aug 2026). Narrative review/opinion synthesis, not new primary data — single-author piece, lower-confidence than a primary study. Confirmed via Crossref + Elsevier. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated.

papers.title: Laxity Comes with Consequences: Connective Tissue Disorders and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth proposes that loose, stretchy connective tissue (as seen in some joint-hypermobility conditions) and ME/CFS can make each other worse in a two-way cycle: low oxygen and overactive immune cells in ME/CFS may weaken the 'glue' that holds collagen fibres together, while pre-existing loose ligaments and an unstable neck can trigger the blood-flow and blood-pressure problems seen in ME/CFS.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure): extends his muscle/blood-flow theory of ME/CFS to connective tissue and joint hypermobility, a link some patients report — but this is an early, not-yet-peer-reviewed hypothesis paper (posted to a preprint server, not medRxiv/bioRxiv), and other researchers have publicly questioned some of its claims, so treat it as a working idea rather than established science.
papers.notes: Solo-author concept/hypothesis paper. Posted May 13, 2026 on Preprints.org (MDPI's preprint platform), version 1, not yet peer-reviewed — a lower-tier venue than medRxiv/bioRxiv, included as an exception because it is Wirth-authored (HIGH priority) per ROUTINE.md. A Science for ME forum commenter raised skepticism about the factual accuracy of some claims — flagged for caution pending peer review.

papers.title: Identification of novel reproducible combinatorial genetic risk factors for myalgic encephalomyelitis in the DecodeME patient cohort and commonalities with long COVID
papers.authors: Sardell J, Das S, Pearson M, Kolobkov D, et al. (PrecisionLife)
papers.summary: Using an AI method that looks at combinations of gene variants (not just single genes), researchers re-analysed the large DecodeME genetic dataset and found over 22,000 reproducible variant-combinations pointing to about 250 'core' genes involved in nerve/brain signalling, inflammation, cell-stress response, and calcium handling; 76 of these genes are also linked to long COVID.
papers.why: A deeper follow-up analysis of the DecodeME genetics study already in this database — it turns raw genetic data into specific biological pathways and proposes two existing drugs (ampligen and apremilast) as candidates worth testing.
papers.notes: Originally posted as medRxiv preprint 2025.12.01.25341362 (Dec 1, 2025); published in J Transl Med Apr 21, 2026. PrecisionLife combinatorial-analytics platform, DecodeME cohort vs UK Biobank controls, replicated across three disjoint DecodeME sub-cohorts. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Companion to decodeme-2025-gwas already in this database.

papers.title: Symptom clusters in ME/CFS reflect distinct neuroimmune and autonomic pathophysiological mechanisms: a translational model
papers.authors: Habermann-Horstmeier L, Horstmeier LM
papers.summary: Studying symptom surveys from 748 German ME/CFS patients, the authors showed that groups of symptoms which tend to occur together (e.g. brain fog, sensory sensitivity, and sleep problems as one group) statistically line up with specific underlying biological processes, such as immune, nerve, or gut-related dysfunction.
papers.why: A German patient-cohort study (the APAV-ME/CFS study) supporting the idea that ME/CFS should be split into biological subgroups rather than treated as one uniform illness — relevant to designing more targeted future drug trials.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 24, article 606 (2026). Published online Apr 28, 2026 (Research Square preprint posted ~Feb 7, 2026). German APAV-ME/CFS cohort, n=748 (608 female, 137 male, 3 non-binary). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated as far as could be confirmed.

papers.title: Mapping the Symptom Profile and Burden of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Insights from the TIMES Survey
papers.authors: Tyson SF, Fleming R
papers.summary: Over 1,000 adults with ME/CFS filled out a detailed symptom questionnaire; on average their overall symptom burden was severe, with cognitive problems (like brain fog) rated the worst and fatigue the most universal symptom, and women reporting a heavier symptom load than men.
papers.why: One of the largest patient-reported symptom-burden surveys in ME/CFS to date; mainly descriptive rather than mechanistic, but useful for quantifying how disabling the illness is across body systems and for designing outcome measures for future drug trials.
papers.notes: medRxiv preprint posted Jun 17, 2026. n=1,028 adults with ME/CFS via the TIMES (The Index of ME Symptoms) questionnaire. Not yet peer-reviewed. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Borderline scope (patient-reported survey, similar to eckey-2025-treatment-outcomes already in this database) — included for completeness, normal priority.

papers.title: Indistinguishable mitochondrial phenotypes after exposure of healthy myoblasts to myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome or control serum
papers.authors: Ryback AA, Hillier CB, Loureiro CM, Ponting CP, Dalton CF
papers.summary: A large, carefully pre-planned study tried to repeat a well-known 2016 finding that blood serum from ME/CFS patients changes how healthy muscle cells produce energy. Using blood from 67 patients and 53 healthy people and over 1,700 lab measurements, they found no such difference this time.
papers.why: A rigorous negative replication from Chris Ponting's group (who also leads the DecodeME genetics study already in this database) — it challenges a widely-cited piece of evidence for a 'blood-borne factor' in ME/CFS and shows the field is actively re-testing its own key claims.
papers.notes: PMID 41632778. PLOS ONE, published Feb 3 2026. Pre-registered attempted replication of a 2016 finding (Tomas et al./Newcastle) re serum effects on myoblast mitochondrial function; found no significant difference vs healthy control serum. Ponting is also senior author of DecodeME (decodeme-2025-gwas, already in this file).

papers.title: Exploring differences in protein cargo of extracellular vesicles from ME/CFS patient plasma compared to healthy controls
papers.authors: Rydland A, Yran ES, Nyman TA, Strand EB, Trøseid AS, Øvstebø R, Heinicke F, Lie BA, Viken MK
papers.summary: Looked at tiny particles that cells shed into the blood (extracellular vesicles) in 49 ME/CFS patients versus 50 healthy people. Patients had more of these particles overall, and a handful of the proteins they carried differed, though none of those individual differences held up after strict statistical checking.
papers.why: The largest such extracellular-vesicle study in ME/CFS so far; a mostly exploratory result, but it adds a new (Norwegian) patient group to this growing biomarker approach, alongside similar work already in this database from the Scheibenbogen group.
papers.notes: PMID 42375682. Biochem Biophys Rep, published online Jun 20 2026 (eCollection Sep 2026). Oslo University Hospital / University of Oslo group. Distinct cohort from the Charité/Scheibenbogen extracellular-vesicle paper (seifert-2026-extracellular-vesicle-biomarker) already in this database.

papers.title: Toward a Molecular Reclassification of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Integrating Multi-Omics, Machine Learning, and Precision Medicine
papers.authors: Frank J, Nesterovitch N, Movva C, Klimas NG, Nathanson L
papers.summary: Reviews how new technologies that can read thousands of gene and protein signals at once are being used to sort ME/CFS patients into distinct biological groups — defined by what is going wrong in their bodies — rather than by symptoms alone, using artificial intelligence to find the patterns.
papers.why: Lays out a roadmap for 'precision medicine' in ME/CFS — where each patient subgroup receives treatment matched to their specific biology — and identifies overactive innate immunity, exhausted immune T cells, and cellular energy failure as the likeliest targets for the first such treatments. From leading US ME/CFS researcher Nancy Klimas's group.
papers.notes: PMID 42196410. Int J Mol Sci 27(10):4436. Published May 15, 2026. Frank (Nova Southeastern University, Klimas group) et al. Comprehensive review covering multi-omics (transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics), machine learning diagnostics (monocyte subsets, cell-free RNA), and precision medicine approaches; identifies innate immune activation, CD8+ T cell exhaustion with TOX/EOMES upregulation, and mitochondrial dysfunction as key molecular signatures.

papers.title: Comparative Gut Microbiome Alterations in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Long COVID-19 Syndrome
papers.authors: Donchev D, Nikolova R, Vaseva K, Taskov H, Murdjeva M, Maes M, Ivanov IN
papers.summary: Directly compared the gut bacteria of ME/CFS patients and long COVID patients, finding shared changes — particularly missing 'good' bacteria and excess of others — that were not seen in healthy people.
papers.why: The first head-to-head comparison of gut microbiome changes in ME/CFS and long COVID; the overlap supports the idea that both conditions share underlying gut-related biology, pointing toward shared treatment strategies such as gut microbiome repair.
papers.notes: Biomedicines 2026, 14(6), 1183. Published May 22, 2026. PMID: 42351611. Bulgarian/international group.

papers.title: Development and validation of blood-based diagnostic biomarkers for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) using EpiSwitch® 3-dimensional genomic regulatory immuno-genetic profiling
papers.authors: Hunter E, Alshaker H, Bundock O, Weston C, Bautista S, Gebregzabhar A, Virdi A, Croxford J, Dring A, Powell R, Vugrinec D, Kingdon C, Wilson C, Dowrick S, Green J, Akoulitchev A, Pchejetski D
papers.summary: Developed and validated a blood test using a novel technique that reads three-dimensional patterns of DNA folding; the test correctly identified ME/CFS patients versus healthy people with 96% accuracy in an independent test group.
papers.why: One of the highest-accuracy diagnostic blood tests ever reported for ME/CFS — a disease that currently has no objective diagnostic test — and reveals specific immune and brain-inflammation pathways as potential drug targets.
papers.notes: PMID: 41057909. Published October 8, 2025. J Transl Med 23:1186 (2025). University of East Anglia / Oxford Biodynamics. A 200-marker EpiSwitch CFS test; sensitivity 92%, specificity 98%, overall accuracy 96%. PMC12506310.

papers.title: Heightened innate immunity may trigger chronic inflammation, fatigue and post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS
papers.authors: Che X, Ranjan A, Guo C, Zhang K, Goldsmith R, Levine S, Moneghetti KJ, Zhai Y, Ge L, Mishra N, Hornig M, Bateman L, Klimas NG, Montoya JG, Peterson DL, Klein SL, Fiehn O, Komaroff AL, Lipkin WI
papers.summary: Found that immune cells from ME/CFS patients overreact to signals from bacteria and viruses — producing far more inflammation-driving molecules than healthy controls — and that this overreaction is linked to disrupted energy production and gut bacteria imbalances.
papers.why: A large multi-institutional study (led by Ian Lipkin at Columbia) that pins down overactive 'first-response' immunity as a key driver of ME/CFS symptoms, and identifies several existing drugs — including metformin and rapamycin — as possible treatments to test.
papers.notes: npj Metab Health Dis 3(1):34. Published September 3, 2025. Multi-centre: Columbia University (Lipkin/Hornig), Stanford (Montoya), Nova Southeastern (Klimas), UC Davis (Bateman), etc. Also preprinted medRxiv 2025.07.23.25332049.

papers.title: Patient-reported treatment outcomes in ME/CFS and long COVID
papers.authors: Eckey M, Li P, Morrison B, Bergquist J, Davis RW, Xiao W
papers.summary: A survey of nearly 4,000 patients across ME/CFS and long COVID asked what helped them from over 150 treatments; people with both conditions reported remarkably similar responses — and graded exercise therapy was rated least helpful.
papers.why: The largest real-world treatment survey in ME/CFS/long COVID, showing the two conditions behave similarly and pointing to which symptom subtypes (e.g. autonomic, cognitive) respond best to which drug classes — directly useful for designing future trials.
papers.notes: PNAS 122(28):e2426874122. PMID: 40627388. Published July 8–15, 2025. MGH / Harvard / Uppsala. Ronald Davis (Stanford OMF) is senior co-author. PMC12280984.

papers.title: Pathophysiological, Translational, and Diagnostic Aspects of ME/CFS: A Focus on Skeletal Muscle Involvement
papers.authors: Fanò-Illic G, Coscia F, Gigliotti PV, Checcaglini F, Carraro U, Fulle S, Mancinelli R
papers.summary: A detailed review of how muscles in ME/CFS fail — they receive too little blood, build up harmful levels of sodium and calcium, produce too much oxidative stress, and lose their normal ability to contract — and how these changes might be detected by standard tests.
papers.why: Integrates molecular, cellular, and clinical evidence into a single picture of why ME/CFS muscles don't work normally, and proposes markers that could be used for diagnosis — supporting the muscle-focused treatment approach being pursued by researchers including Wirth and Scheibenbogen.
papers.notes: Diagnostics 2026, 16(7), 1019. Published March 28, 2026. Narrative review covering literature 1990–2025. Authors: Fanò-Illic (Univ. G. d'Annunzio, Chieti, Italy) et al. Not by Wirth/Scheibenbogen but closely related to their muscle-energy hypothesis.

papers.title: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves clinical symptoms and functional capacity and modulates thalamic connectivity in ME/CFS: a prospective cohort study
papers.authors: Kim L, Cammà G, Peters CK, Mantwill M, Müller O, Leprêtre N, Heindrich C, Rust R, Krill M, Hartung TJ, Reeß LG, Krohn S, Heymann CV, Wittke K, Finke C, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: ME/CFS patients who received hyperbaric oxygen treatment (breathing pure oxygen in a pressurised chamber) showed improved symptoms and physical function; brain scans also revealed changes in an area linked to fatigue.
papers.why: Involves Carmen Scheibenbogen's team and is one of the first studies to link symptom improvement with measurable brain changes after oxygen treatment — potentially pointing to both a therapy and a biological marker of response.
papers.notes: PMID 42249466. Published June 5, 2026. J Transl Med 24(1):744. Scheibenbogen is senior co-author — HIGH PRIORITY. Linked to completed trial NCT06118138 at Charité Berlin.

papers.title: Low Vasopressin in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Huhmar HM, Soinne LS, Bertilson BC, Ghatan PH, Bragée BA, Polo OJ
papers.summary: Found that levels of vasopressin — a hormone that helps control water balance, blood flow, and stress responses — were lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy people.
papers.why: Low vasopressin could help explain symptoms like dizziness, excessive thirst, and fatigue, and may become a diagnostic marker or a target for treatment.
papers.notes: PMID 41475665. Epub Dec 29 2025; print Jun 2026. Endocr Pract 32(6):902-908.

papers.title: Dynamic microclot profiling: thromboelastography advances precision management in long COVID and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Saleem S, Hussain A, Haroon M, Raza A, Afzal U, Anwar MF, Imran S, Iqbal MU, Hajj F
papers.summary: Used a specialised clotting test to measure tiny blood clots (microclots) in long COVID and ME/CFS patients, finding different clotting patterns among individuals that could guide personalised treatment.
papers.why: Adds to the growing evidence that abnormal clotting and poor circulation contribute to ME/CFS; the profiling method it describes could help identify which patients might benefit from anti-clotting therapies.
papers.notes: PMID 42274123. Published online June 11, 2026. Blood Coagul Fibrinolysis (ahead of print).

papers.title: Imbalance of Excitatory and Inhibitory Neurotransmitter Systems in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: Reviews evidence that ME/CFS disturbs the brain's chemical messengers — the signals nerve cells use to talk to each other — which may explain symptoms like brain fog and feeling 'wired but tired'.
papers.why: From the two leading German ME/CFS researchers: it links the disease's effects in the muscles to its effects in the brain, reinforcing the case for the treatments they are developing.
papers.notes: PMID 42123618. Published April 30, 2026. Int J Mol Sci 27(9):4041.

papers.title: Charting the circulating proteome in ME/CFS using cross-system profiling to uncover mechanistic insights
papers.authors: Hoel A, Hoel F, Dyrstad SE, Chapola H, Rekeland IG, Risa K, Alme K, Sørland K, Brokstad KA, Marti HP, Mella O, Fluge Ø, Tronstad KJ
papers.summary: Measured thousands of proteins in patients' blood and found many that differ from healthy people — signs of an overactive immune system and poor blood flow to the muscles.
papers.why: The largest blood-protein study in ME/CFS so far; it maps what is going wrong in the body and could lead to a blood test and new treatment targets.
papers.notes: Published March 4, 2026. From the Fluge/Mella group (Bergen, Norway).

papers.title: Proteomic signatures in cerebrospinal fluid and their clinical associations in patients with ME/CFS
papers.authors: Bragée B, Li P, Meadows D, et al.
papers.summary: Examined proteins in the fluid that bathes the brain and spinal cord, and found inflammation-related patterns that matched how severe patients were and whether they also had a racing heart on standing up (a condition called POTS).
papers.why: One of the first studies of this fluid in ME/CFS; the patterns it found could become markers for sorting patients into the right treatment groups.

papers.title: Pathophysiological mechanisms of post-exertional malaise: an integrative analysis based on the metabolism-immune-neuro interaction model
papers.authors: Jin H, An Y, Huang J, Luo T, Wu X
papers.summary: Proposes how even light activity can trigger a 'crash' (the delayed worsening of symptoms after exertion, called post-exertional malaise): the cells' energy units falter, this sparks inflammation, and the inflammation reaches the brain and keeps the cycle going.
papers.why: Offers a clear, testable explanation for ME/CFS's defining symptom — crashing after exertion — and points toward energy- and inflammation-based treatments.
papers.notes: Published April 13, 2026. Frontiers in Immunology vol. 17.

papers.title: Elevated serum levels of interleukin-11 and matrix metalloproteinase-9 in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Chinnappan B, Kempuraj D, Aenlle KK, Middleton A, Day KS, Kothuru SP, Joshi RS, Klimas NG, Theoharides TC
papers.summary: Found two inflammation-related substances raised in patients' blood, and linked them to immune cells reacting to the Epstein–Barr virus (the cause of glandular fever).
papers.why: These substances could serve as a blood marker, and the link to a common virus hints at new treatment ideas.
papers.notes: Published June 5, 2026. PMID 42327760.

papers.title: Large-scale investigation confirms TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Sasso EM, Er TS, Eaton-Fitch N, Hool L, Muraki K, Marshall-Gradisnik S
papers.summary: Confirmed, across several laboratories, that a tiny 'gate' which lets calcium into certain immune cells doesn't work properly in ME/CFS patients.
papers.why: Because independent labs got the same result, this faulty cell 'gate' is one of the most reliable biological signs of ME/CFS and a possible drug target.
papers.notes: Published January 8, 2026. Frontiers in Medicine vol. 12.

papers.title: Plasma cell targeting with the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — a clinical pilot study
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Rekeland IG, Sørland K, Alme K, Risa K, Bruland O, Tronstad KJ, Mella O
papers.summary: A small trial gave 10 patients daratumumab — a drug that clears the immune cells which make antibodies; 6 of 10 improved and several stayed better for one to two years.
papers.why: The first trial of this approach in ME/CFS; the strong, lasting improvement supports the idea that misguided antibodies drive the illness, and a larger trial is planned.
papers.notes: Published July 9, 2025. Fluge/Mella group, Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen, Norway.

papers.title: Safety, tolerability and clinical effects of rovunaptabin (BC007) on fatigue and quality of life in patients with Post-COVID syndrome (reCOVer): a phase IIa randomised controlled trial
papers.authors: Hohberger B, Ganslmayer M, Harrer T, et al.
papers.summary: In a rigorous trial with a placebo group, a drug that neutralises harmful 'self-attacking' antibodies reduced fatigue and improved quality of life in Long COVID patients.
papers.why: The first properly controlled trial showing benefit from removing these antibodies — strong support for antibody-targeting treatments that are also being explored in ME/CFS.
papers.notes: Published July 22, 2025. University Hospital Erlangen, Germany. This is the reCOVer trial result.

papers.title: Key Pathophysiological Role of Skeletal Muscle Disturbance in Post COVID and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Accumulated Evidence
papers.authors: Scheibenbogen C, Wirth KJ
papers.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
papers.summary: Pulls together evidence that ME/CFS muscles get too little blood and build up salt (sodium) and calcium, which damages the muscle cells' energy units.
papers.why: A cornerstone of the Wirth/Scheibenbogen theory and the direct rationale for their drug MDC002, which aims to fix exactly this muscle problem.
papers.notes: Published February 2025. PMID 39727052. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 16(1). Wirth + Scheibenbogen joint review.

papers.title: Expert perspectives on myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — Insights from the 3rd International Conference of the Charité Fatigue Center
papers.authors: Fehrer A, et al.
papers.summary: Summarises what experts at Charité's international ME/CFS conference agree on — problems with circulation, the immune system, and the body's energy use — and warns that steady research funding is urgently needed.
papers.why: Lays out the Scheibenbogen group's current priorities and the thinking behind their trials (immunoadsorption and the planned inebilizumab study).
papers.notes: PMID 41895458. Lead author Annick Fehrer, Charité Berlin. Epub March 25 2026. Confirmed via Elsevier.

papers.title: Tryptophan Metabolism and Aryl-Hydrocarbon Receptor Agonists in the Gut Microbiome of People With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Esteban DJ, Conrad B, Cullinan A, et al.
papers.summary: Found that the gut bacteria of ME/CFS patients handle the nutrient tryptophan differently, making fewer of the molecules that help keep the immune system calm.
papers.why: Points to the gut as a possible lever on the immune system, supporting microbiome- and immune-based treatment ideas.
papers.notes: PMID 42325052. Microbiologyopen 15(3):e70333. Confirmed via PubMed.

papers.title: Systems neuroendocrinology in ME/CFS and long COVID: a chronobiological framework for hormone-based research
papers.authors: Thomas N, Huang K, Schneider-Futschik EK, et al.
papers.summary: Argues that hormone studies in ME/CFS and Long COVID disagree because they ignore differences by time of day and menstrual-cycle phase, and recommends accounting for these.
papers.why: Better-designed hormone studies could uncover treatment targets; gives practical guidance for trials, especially those with mostly female participants.
papers.notes: PMID 42320559. Front Neuroendocrinol. Confirmed via PubMed.

papers.title: Gastrointestinal symptoms correlate with core clinical features and systemic inflammation in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Brown M, Vernon SD, Indart AC, Green PH, Alaedini A
papers.summary: Showed that the worse a patient's gut symptoms are, the worse their main ME/CFS symptoms and body-wide inflammation tend to be — suggesting the gut is part of the disease, not a side issue.
papers.why: Supports treating gut problems as central to ME/CFS, which could shape who is enrolled in drug trials and how improvement is measured.
papers.notes: PMID 42321833. J Transl Med. Confirmed via PubMed.

papers.title: A Unifying Hypothesis of the Pathophysiology of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Recognitions from the finding of autoantibodies against ß2-adrenergic receptors
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: Proposes one framework that ties ME/CFS together: 'self-attacking' antibodies against receptors that control blood vessels lead to poor blood flow and too little oxygen reaching muscles and brain.
papers.why: The central Wirth/Scheibenbogen theory — it underpins their drug MDC002 and the autoantibody-removal treatments now being tested.
papers.notes: Autoimmun Rev 19(4):102527. Landmark Wirth + Scheibenbogen hypothesis paper.

papers.title: Pathophysiology of skeletal muscle disturbances in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: Explains in detail how poor blood flow and a buildup of sodium and calcium could damage how ME/CFS muscles make energy.
papers.why: Builds the muscle-level mechanism behind the Wirth/Scheibenbogen theory and the rationale for their drug MDC002.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 19(1):162. PMID 33882940. Wirth + Scheibenbogen.

papers.title: Antibodies to β adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors in patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Loebel M, Grabowski P, Heidecke H, et al. (Scheibenbogen C, senior author)
papers.summary: Found that many ME/CFS patients carry raised 'self-attacking' antibodies against receptors that control blood vessels and the nervous system.
papers.why: A foundational finding for the autoimmune theory of ME/CFS and the basis for treatments that remove these antibodies (immunoadsorption, BC007). From the Scheibenbogen group.
papers.notes: Brain Behav Immun 52:32-39. PMID 26399744. Scheibenbogen group.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome — Evidence for an autoimmune disease
papers.authors: Sotzny F, Blanco J, Capelli E, Castro-Marrero J, Steiner S, Murovska M, Scheibenbogen C (EUROMENE)
papers.summary: A review gathering the evidence that ME/CFS — at least in a subgroup of patients — behaves like an autoimmune disease, where the immune system attacks the body.
papers.why: Framed the autoimmune model that drives much of today's treatment research. From the Scheibenbogen group / European EUROMENE network.
papers.notes: Autoimmun Rev 17(6):601-609. Scheibenbogen group.

papers.title: Endothelial dysfunction and altered endothelial biomarkers in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Haffke M, Freitag H, Rudolf G, et al. (Scheibenbogen C, Sotzny F)
papers.summary: Found that the inner lining of blood vessels (the endothelium) doesn't work properly in many ME/CFS and Long COVID patients.
papers.why: Supports the idea that poor blood-vessel function drives ME/CFS symptoms, and points to treatments that target the vessels. From the Scheibenbogen group.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 20(1):138. PMID 35317812. Scheibenbogen group.

papers.title: Human Herpesvirus-6 Reactivation, Mitochondrial Fragmentation, and the Coordination of Antiviral and Metabolic Phenotypes in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Schreiner P, Harrer T, Scheibenbogen C, Lamer S, Schlosser A, Naviaux RK, Prusty BK
papers.summary: Suggests that reactivation of a common herpesvirus (HHV-6) can shatter cells' energy factories (mitochondria), switching the body into a protective but energy-starved state.
papers.why: Connects a viral trigger to the energy failure seen in ME/CFS — a possible mechanism linking an old infection to lasting illness. Co-authored by Scheibenbogen, Naviaux and Prusty.
papers.notes: ImmunoHorizons 4(4):201-215. PMID 32327453. Scheibenbogen co-author.

papers.title: Initial findings from the DecodeME genome-wide association study of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Ponting CP, et al. (DecodeME Consortium)
papers.summary: The largest genetic study of ME/CFS (over 15,000 patients) found eight spots in our DNA linked to the illness, several involved in how the body fights infection.
papers.why: First strong genetic evidence that ME/CFS has a biological basis involving the immune and nervous systems — and a source of new drug targets.
papers.notes: medRxiv 2025.08.06.25333109. Led by Chris Ponting, Univ. of Edinburgh. Preprint (peer review pending).

papers.title: Deep phenotyping of post-infectious myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Walitt B, Singh K, et al. (NIH intramural study)
papers.summary: An intensive US National Institutes of Health study found measurable brain, immune and metabolic differences in people whose ME/CFS began after an infection.
papers.why: A high-profile government study confirming the illness has real biological abnormalities (though its 'effort preference' wording was controversial among patients).
papers.notes: Nat Commun 15:907. PMID 38383456. NIH intramural deep-phenotyping cohort.

papers.title: AI-driven multi-omics modeling of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Xiong R, Aiken E, Caldwell R, Vernon SD, Kozhaya L, Gunter C, Bateman L, Unutmaz D, Oh J
papers.summary: Used artificial intelligence on four years of layered biological data (gut, blood, immune, metabolism) to pick out ME/CFS biomarkers and predict how severe symptoms are.
papers.why: A cutting-edge, data-driven map of the disease that could improve diagnosis and reveal new mechanisms.
papers.notes: Nat Med 2025. 'BioMapAI' deep neural network. Jackson Laboratory (Oh/Unutmaz) + Bateman Horne Center.

papers.title: Circulating cell-free RNA signatures for the characterization and diagnosis of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Gardella AE, Eweis-LaBolle D, Loy CJ, et al. (Hanson MR, De Vlaminck I)
papers.summary: A blood test reading fragments of genetic material (RNA) floating in plasma told ME/CFS patients from healthy people with about 77% accuracy, and flagged immune and platelet differences.
papers.why: A promising step toward an objective blood test for a disease that currently has none, plus fresh clues about immune involvement. Cornell (Hanson) group.
papers.notes: PNAS 122 (2025). PMID 40789036. Cornell (Hanson) / De Vlaminck.

papers.title: Metabolic features of chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Naviaux RK, Naviaux JC, Li K, et al.
papers.summary: Found that ME/CFS patients' blood chemistry shows a widespread 'slowed-down' metabolism — the body acting as if in a low-energy survival mode.
papers.why: A widely-cited study arguing ME/CFS is a measurable disorder of how the body makes and uses energy, not a psychological problem.

papers.title: Metabolic profiling indicates impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase function in myalgic encephalopathy/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Mella O, Bruland O, et al.
papers.summary: Blood chemistry pointed to a blocked step in how cells turn food into energy — a key enzyme (pyruvate dehydrogenase) appears to be held back.
papers.why: A concrete, testable defect in energy production that could explain the exhaustion and serve as a drug target. Bergen (Fluge/Mella) group.
papers.notes: JCI Insight 1(21):e89376. PMID 28018972.

papers.title: Cytokine signature associated with disease severity in chronic fatigue syndrome patients
papers.authors: Montoya JG, Holmes TH, Anderson JN, et al. (Davis MM)
papers.summary: Levels of several immune-signaling molecules (cytokines) in the blood rose in step with how severe a patient's ME/CFS was.
papers.why: Links the immune system directly to symptom severity and points to inflammation-based markers and treatments. Stanford group.

papers.title: Distinct plasma immune signatures in ME/CFS are present early in the course of illness
papers.authors: Hornig M, Montoya JG, Klimas NG, et al. (Lipkin WI)
papers.summary: Patients ill for under three years had a distinctive blood immune pattern that faded in those ill longer — showing the disease has stages.
papers.why: Early hard evidence that ME/CFS is biological and changes over time, and a hint that treating early might matter. Columbia (Lipkin) group.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in Patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: An 11C-(R)-PK11195 PET Study
papers.authors: Nakatomi Y, Mizuno K, Ishii A, et al.
papers.summary: Brain scans showed signs of inflammation (activated immune cells) in several brain regions of ME/CFS patients.
papers.why: Among the first direct evidence of brain inflammation in ME/CFS, supporting the 'encephalomyelitis' (brain inflammation) part of the disease's name.
papers.notes: J Nucl Med 55(6):945-950. RIKEN, Japan.

papers.title: Insights From Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing of Patients With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Joseph P, Arevalo C, Oliveira RKF, et al. (Systrom DM)
papers.summary: Using exercise tests with catheters in the blood vessels, found that ME/CFS patients' blood doesn't return and circulate properly during exertion ('preload failure'), alongside nerve abnormalities.
papers.why: Gives a physical, measurable explanation for exercise intolerance and points to circulation- and nerve-targeted treatments. Harvard (Systrom) group.

papers.title: Inability of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome patients to reproduce VO2peak indicates functional impairment
papers.authors: Keller BA, Pryor JL, Giloteaux L
papers.summary: On two exercise tests 24 hours apart, ME/CFS patients could not match their day-1 performance on day 2 — an objective sign of the 'crash' after exertion.
papers.why: Provides an objective, measurable test of post-exertional malaise — important for diagnosis and disability assessment.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 12:104. PMID 24755065. Two-day CPET.

papers.title: Reduced diversity and altered composition of the gut microbiome in individuals with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Giloteaux L, Goodrich JK, Walters WA, Levine SM, Ley RE, Hanson MR
papers.summary: ME/CFS patients had less varied gut bacteria and signs of a 'leaky' gut letting microbes into the bloodstream.
papers.why: Early evidence linking the gut microbiome to ME/CFS, opening microbiome-based diagnosis and treatment ideas. Cornell (Hanson) group.
papers.notes: Microbiome 4:30. PMID 27338587.

papers.title: Multi-'omics of gut microbiome-host interactions in short- and long-term myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome patients
papers.authors: Xiong R, Gunter C, Fleming E, et al. (Hanson MR, Oh J, Unutmaz D)
papers.summary: A detailed gut analysis showed ME/CFS patients lack bacteria that make butyrate (a fuel that nourishes the gut lining); the pattern differed depending on how long they had been ill.
papers.why: One of the most rigorous microbiome studies in ME/CFS, strengthening the gut-disease link and possible treatments.
papers.notes: Cell Host Microbe 31(2):273-287. Companion paper to Guo et al. 2023.

papers.title: A nanoelectronics-blood-based diagnostic biomarker for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Esfandyarpour R, Kashi A, Nemat-Gorgani M, Wilhelmy J, Davis RW
papers.summary: A tiny electronic 'nanoneedle' blood test separated ME/CFS patients from healthy people by how their cells cope with stress.
papers.why: A candidate objective diagnostic test for a disease that currently has none. Stanford / Open Medicine Foundation (Davis) group.

papers.title: B-Lymphocyte Depletion in Patients With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial (RituxME)
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Rekeland IG, Lien K, et al. (Mella O)
papers.summary: A large, rigorous trial of rituximab — a drug that wipes out B-cells (an immune cell type) — found it did NOT help ME/CFS patients overall.
papers.why: A pivotal negative result that ended hopes for rituximab and redirected the field; a landmark in ME/CFS research history. Bergen (Fluge/Mella) group.
papers.notes: Ann Intern Med 170(9):585-593. The definitive phase-3 RituxME trial (negative).

papers.title: Intravenous Cyclophosphamide in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. An Open-Label Phase II Study
papers.authors: Rekeland IG, Fosså A, Lande A, et al. (Fluge Ø, Mella O)
papers.summary: An open-label study (no placebo group) of the immune-suppressing drug cyclophosphamide reported that about half of ME/CFS patients improved.
papers.why: An early signal that calming the immune system may help some patients — needs placebo-controlled confirmation, but supports the autoimmune treatment line.
papers.notes: Front Med 7:162. PMID 32411717. Bergen (Fluge/Mella) group.

papers.title: Insights from myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome may help unravel the pathogenesis of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Komaroff AL, Lipkin WI
papers.summary: A review arguing that Long COVID and ME/CFS likely share the same underlying biology.
papers.why: Helped place ME/CFS at the centre of Long COVID research, bringing the field new attention and funding.
papers.notes: Trends Mol Med 27(9):895-906.

papers.title: Myalgic encephalomyelitis: International Consensus Criteria
papers.authors: Carruthers BM, van de Sande MI, De Meirleir KL, et al.
papers.summary: An international expert panel defined stricter ways to diagnose the illness, centred on symptoms getting worse after exertion, and recommended dropping the name 'chronic fatigue syndrome'.
papers.why: Widely-used research and clinical criteria that put the disease's hallmark feature — post-exertional worsening — at the centre of diagnosis.
papers.notes: J Intern Med 270(4):327-338. The 'ICC' criteria.

papers.title: Beyond Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Redefining an Illness
papers.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee (National Academies)
papers.summary: A major US expert panel concluded ME/CFS is a serious physical disease, proposed simpler diagnostic criteria, and suggested renaming it 'systemic exertion intolerance disease' (SEID).
papers.why: A landmark report that medically legitimised the illness and reshaped how it is diagnosed.
papers.notes: IOM/National Academy of Medicine report, Feb 2015. NCBI Bookshelf NBK274235. Proposed the SEID criteria.

papers.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME)
papers.authors: Lim EJ, Ahn YC, Jang ES, et al.
papers.summary: Pooled dozens of studies to estimate how common ME/CFS is worldwide (roughly 0.5–1% of people, depending on the definition used).
papers.why: Establishes the scale of the disease — many millions affected — strengthening the case for research funding and services.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 18:100.

papers.title: Immunoglobulin G complexes from post-infectious ME/CFS, including post-COVID ME/CFS disrupt cellular energetics and alter inflammatory marker secretion
papers.authors: Liu Z, Hollmann C, Kalanidhi S, Lamer S, Schlosser A, Basens EE, Nikolayshvili G, Sokolovska L, Riemekasten G, Rust R, Bellmann-Strobl J, Paul F, Naviaux RK, Nora-Krukle Z, Sotzny F, Scheibenbogen C, Prusty BK
papers.summary: Antibodies (immune proteins called IgG) taken from ME/CFS patients' blood were shown to shatter the energy-producing structures inside blood-vessel cells and change the cells' inflammatory signals.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen and Prusty: directly demonstrates that ME/CFS antibodies damage cellular energy machinery — supporting antibody-removing treatments such as immunoadsorption and highlighting why patients' blood vessels may not function normally.
papers.notes: PMID 41704659. Brain Behav Immun Health. Published Feb 4 2026 (print Mar 2026). Scheibenbogen (Charité) + Prusty (Würzburg) as senior authors. 106-participant study.

papers.title: Extracellular Vesicle Protein and MiRNA Signatures as Biomarkers for Post-Infectious ME/CFS Patients
papers.authors: Seifert M, Schäfers J, Douglas FF, Schwarzburg C, Boristowski D, Birke A, Klein O, Sotzny F, Rubarth K, Windzio L, Beez CM, Kedor Peters C, Wittke K, Scheibenbogen C, Greco A
papers.summary: Tiny particles shed by blood cells (extracellular vesicles) carry distinctive protein and genetic signals in ME/CFS patients, and lower levels of one small genetic molecule (microRNA let-7b-5p) were linked to worse fatigue and pain.
papers.why: From the Scheibenbogen group: these vesicle-based markers could become a blood test for ME/CFS and help separate patients into subgroups for more targeted treatment.
papers.notes: PMID 41828537. Int J Mol Sci 27(5):2314. Published Feb 28 2026. Scheibenbogen (Charité) senior co-author.

papers.title: A causal link between autoantibodies and neurological symptoms in long COVID
papers.authors: Santos Guedes de Sá K, Silva J, Bayarri-Olmos R, et al. (Iwasaki A, senior author)
papers.summary: Antibodies produced during COVID infection persist in long COVID patients and, when transferred into mice, caused fatigue, coordination problems, and nerve damage — proving these 'self-attacking' antibodies directly cause neurological symptoms.
papers.why: High-impact proof (in Cell, one of science's top journals) that autoantibodies physically cause post-viral illness — directly supports the antibody-removing treatments being developed for ME/CFS.
papers.notes: PMID 42208499. Cell 189(11):3214-3235.e37. Published May 28 2026. Iwasaki lab (Yale). Directly supports GPCR autoantibody hypothesis underlying Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption trials.

papers.title: The potential causes of myasthenia and fasciculations in severely ill ME/CFS patients: the role of disturbed electrophysiology
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Steinacker JM
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth proposes that muscle weakness, cramps, and twitching in severely ill ME/CFS patients all arise from one underlying problem: an energy pump in muscle membranes fails, triggering a cascade of excess calcium and electrical instability.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure): the mechanism described is exactly what his drug MDC002 aims to fix, making this a direct scientific rationale for the planned MDC002 Phase 1 trial.
papers.notes: PMID 41705124. Front Physiol (2025 article collection, published Feb 2 2026). Wirth (Mitodicure) + Steinacker. HIGH PRIORITY — Wirth authored.

papers.title: Irisin Signaling Resistance in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: A Proposed Mechanistic Framework for Post-Exertional Malaise Involving the TSP-1-HSP90α-αvβ5 Axis
papers.authors: Souma B, Elremaly W, Akoume MY, Elbakry M, Godbout C, Moreau A
papers.summary: ME patients had lower levels of irisin (a hormone normally released by exercise) and an abnormal response when it was present, blocked by another protein called thrombospondin-1 — pointing to a new molecular explanation for why any exertion triggers a crash.
